segments: [page 366] ...former days, and the favors that the House of Zengi had bestowed upon him.
And they also wept before him,
and took hold of his skirts.
He, however, did not accept their plea,
and put their hopes to shame.
When he departed and they fell into despair,
the people of Mosul, both great and small, were stirred with zeal,
and showed love for the House of the Atabeg Zengi.
With all their heart and soul they manned the walls,
and fought valiantly,
hurling words of insult allusively at Saladin, as one who wronged the benefactor of his lords.
Therefore, he left an army against Mosul to besiege it (or: subdue it),
and he himself went against Khilat,
because he had heard that the Shah-Arman, its ruler, had passed away,
and a slave of his, Bektimur, had risen up in his place,
and treated the people of Khilat well,
and they loved him greatly.
Now this Bektimur,
because he heard that Pahlawan son of Ildeguz {OCR?}, the ruler of Persia, was advancing against him,
sent to Saladin asking him to come to his aid,
promising to surrender Khilat to him.
When Saladin came to the territory of Khilat,
he found that Bektimur had fortified himself in his city,
and did not come out to meet him.
Shams al-Din Pahlawan also arrived from Persia,
and encamped on the other side of Khilat.
He was preparing to wage war against Khilat, had it not been said to him:
"If you press Bektimur hard,
he will surrender Khilat to Saladin,
and you will find no peace in having him as a neighbor."
Therefore, Pahlawan sent to Bektimur and cheered his heart,
and gave him also a woman from among the daughters (sons) of his race in marriage,
and he departed and went away.
When Saladin saw that the people of Khilat and the Persians had become reconciled,
he turned back and came against Mayyafariqin,
because its lord, Qutb al-Din, the lord of Mardin, had died,
and he had made his young son king, as we have related,
and he waged war against it.
There was in it the commander of the army, Asad al-Din Bariqas {OCR?},
and also the Khatun, the wife of Qutb al-Din, the lord of Mardin, was there with her daughters,
and she greatly encouraged the fighters within.
And when the war dragged on—
[Footnote: ] Bektamar,
Bektamur,
Bukhtamar,
Bukhtmur, etc.
Everywhere we write Bektimur,
which is known today among us.
